item.title: When Singles' Day shoppers start stocking up on AI tokens, the time has changed: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 00:30:00
Concept picture of Token Photo: VCG As ordinary Chinese consumers embrace AI and enjoy the convenience of stockpiling tokens through e-commerce livestreams, and as humanoid robots and green manufacturing emerge as new showcases of China's intelligent manufacturing capabilities and Chinese modernization, an increasing number of Western media outlets and scholars are coming to recognize a remarkable reality: "The future is in China." This year's Double 11, or Singles' Day, shopping festival has brought a new item to Chinese consumers' shopping lists: Token. Tmall and JD.com have each introduced AI token sections bringing together services from Alibaba Cloud, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Zhipu AI. One livestream even recorded sales of 2 trillion tokens in just half an hour. The fact that AI tokens have become one of the headline products on e-commerce platforms is a phenomenon rarely seen anywhere else in the world. Foreign media have taken notice, expressing both curiosity and astonishment. There was a time when Americans were driving cars, watching television and eating fried chicken, while the "four big things" in Chinese households were watches, bicycles, sewing machines and radios. It was not until the late 1970s that televisions, refrigerators and washing machines began to find their way into a limited number of Chinese homes. In those days, the West had the power to set the standard for what constituted "modern living," and its way of life was widely regarded as the model for the future. China's priority was to catch up with industrialization, bringing within reach of ordinary households products that had long been commonplace elsewhere. Few could have imagined that, decades later, China would be at the forefront of the widespread adoption of smart devices, mobile payments and digital services. Fewer even could have predicted that China would become a force in defining new forms of consumption, new standards and even new ways of life in the latest wave of digital transformation. The same transformation is also unfolding in digital technology. A new digital product or concept would often first take shape in Silicon Valley before gradually spreading to the rest of the world. But the appearance of tokens on Singles' Day shopping shelves has challenged this long-established pattern. Tokens are no longer simply another overseas concept or business model replicated in China. Instead, the token-based consumption has emerged from the combined forces of China's vast digital consumer market, highly active user base and mature industrial ecosystem. Just a few years ago, some Western commentators were still quick to question China's capacity for digital innovation, arguing that it could make only incremental advances in applications but would never forge its own path in foundational technologies. Yet the rapid uptake of open-source large language models, the gradual deployment of humanoid robots in industrial settings, and now the arrival of digital resources in the mass consumer market tell a different story. The world is witnessing an innovation hub capable of continually defining new demands and creating new applications. As ordinary Chinese consumers embrace AI and enjoy the convenience of stockpiling tokens through e-commerce livestreams, and as humanoid robots and green manufacturing emerge as new showcases of China's intelligent manufacturing capabilities and Chinese modernization, an increasing number of Western media outlets and scholars are coming to recognize a remarkable reality: "The future is in China." Today, AI is not only directly driving consumption of smart devices and related hardware, but the "AI Plus" initiative is also deeply empowering the rapid development of sectors such as education, healthcare, elderly care, culture and tourism, employment, and consumer services. As AI enters millions of households and empowers thousands of industries, a more competitive AI consumer ecosystem will bring more affordable tokens and a wider range of application scenarios. Underpinning this transformation is China's rapid progress in AI foundation models, cloud computing, and the chip application ecosystem. China is developing distinctive competitive advantages in the global AI race. According to OpenRouter, a global AI model aggregation platform, Chinese large language models have outpaced their US counterparts in token usage for 27 consecutive weeks, including the week of October 26 to November 1. More than one-third of the tokens used by enterprises in the Global South countries come from Chinese models. Increasingly, the decisive factor in AI competition is whether companies can consistently deliver reliable, practical AI services to businesses and consumers at reasonable costs, and whether technological advances can be translated into productivity gains across industries. Why has China been among the first to develop an ecosystem for token consumption? The answer is simple: the public's high level of acceptance has accelerated the development of the ecosystem, while a mature ecosystem has, in turn, further reinforced positive public attitudes. A 2025 KPMG survey covering 47 countries found that Chinese people were among the most optimistic about AI. From electronic payments to e-commerce and food delivery, from short videos to intelligent driving, and now to access to highly cost-effective AI tokens, Chinese consumers have undoubtedly been at the forefront of enjoying the benefits of the intelligent era. This positive, self-reinforcing ecosystem is the natural outcome of China's remarkable rise in comprehensive national strength and the broad improvement in its population's educational and cultural attainment over the past several decades. From the "four big things" and "three big things" that once symbolized household prosperity to the integration of digital technologies into everyday consumption today, the Chinese people's pursuit of a better life has never changed. What has changed is our ability and approach to fulfill that aspiration. Today, we are turning the possibilities of a new era of digital civilization into experiences that benefit billions of people globally. This transformation has not been driven by exploitation, coercion, or the erection of barriers, but by practical efforts to ensure that ordinary people can genuinely and equally share in the benefits of technological progress.

item.title: EU approval of JD.com-Ceconomy acquisition shows dialogue works, but concerns over FSR targeting Chinese firms remain: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 23:47:00
China EU Photo:VCG The EU conditionally approved JD.com's acquisition of Germany's Ceconomy under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR) on Tuesday local time, the first Chinese deal cleared after an in-depth probe. Chinese experts said the move shows that both sides can resolve issues through constructive communication, demonstrating that commercial interests continue to overlap. However, the EU is reportedly working on targeted changes to single market rules on foreign subsidies and vehicle type approval to diversify supply chains and reduce reliance on China, according to a Bloomberg report on Tuesday. Analysts noted that these two developments emerging in parallel clearly reflect the EU's current economic policy toward China - retaining a degree of flexibility for specific commercial projects that meet certain conditions, while advancing "de-risking" at the regulatory level. Using "security" as a pretext for protectionism will ultimately only raise Europe's own costs and further erode mutual trust and the foundation for China-EU cooperation, they warned. Acquisition approved, FSR questions remain The European Commission (EC) on Tuesday announced to approve, under the FSR, the acquisition of Ceconomy by JD.com. It marks the first case in which an acquisition by a Chinese company has been approved by the EC following an in-depth investigation under the FSR. Ceconomy CEO Dr Kai-Ulrich Deissner said that "With JD.com's outstanding retail, logistics, and technology capabilities, we can further accelerate our successful growth trajectory and go beyond our current strategic goals." JD.com CEO Sandy Xu noted "This partnership with Ceconomy will build Europe's leading next-generation consumer electronics platform," according to the information JD.com shared with the Global Times on Wednesday. The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) said on Wednesday that it welcomes EC's approval. It said that the decision, reached after extensive engagement with both parties and a comprehensive assessment of the proposed commitments, underscores the importance of constructive dialogue between regulators and businesses in addressing regulatory concerns. Zhang Jian, a vice president of the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the EC's latest move has a positive significance, demonstrating that the importance of constructive dialogue between regulators and businesses in addressing regulatory concerns and the proper handling of the case is conducive to the win-win commercial cooperation between companies from both sides. After entering the European market, JD.com will bring in new capital, technology and industrial elements, which will help boost the performance of local manufacturers and retailers, driving the development of the consumer goods sector, Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Wednesday. However, whether this will set a template for future FSR cases involving Chinese companies remains to be seen, since the underlying logic of the EU's trade and economic policy toward China has not changed, Zhang said. He noted that it is important for the bloc to keep its market fair and objective and avoid discriminating against Chinese companies operating in the EU given their contribution to the EU's growth and job creation. The FSR started to apply in 2023. The EC claimed the FSR enables the Commission to address distortions caused by foreign subsidies and thereby allows the EU to ensure a level playing field for all companies operating in the internal market. However, since the FSR came into force, the vast majority of investigations launched by the EC under the FSR framework have targeted Chinese companies. A growing number of ex officio investigations have also focused primarily on Chinese firms, spanning sectors including wind turbines, security screening equipment, new energy vehicles and e-commerce. "The FSR is not inherently indefensible, but if its enforcement continues to display country-based selectivity, its credibility will be eroded," Jian said. The CCCEU said that the FSR and its implementation remain a key concern for Chinese companies investing in Europe. "Regulatory measures should be tailored to the circumstances of each case, with due regard for businesses' legitimate rights and interests, and should not create unnecessary barriers to legitimate commercial investment or market cooperation," it said. EU's dual-track dilemma China and Europe held high-level talks in Beijing in October that produced positive outcomes, yet the EU has continued to roll out or is brewing new restrictive measures. Bloomberg reported Tuesday that the EU is working on targeted changes to its single market to help domestic companies diversify supply chains away from countries including China, according to people familiar with the plan. The move is part of a broader package of measures the bloc is set to unveil by mid-December. Other plans for the package include a diversification instrument that will aim to nudge businesses toward alternative supplies. In parallel, the EU is reportedly planning to use safeguard measures to cut imports of products from sectors including chemicals, furniture and machinery from China. According to Bloomberg, the EC will seek to amend laws on motor vehicle-type approvals and foreign subsidies to better address economic security risks from some imports while reducing regulatory friction for like-minded foreign suppliers. It will also amend forced labor laws and the trade secrets directive, making it easier for European companies to diversify supply chains within the bloc's internal market and harder for riskier suppliers to access it, according to the report. Jian said that on the one hand, the EU is raising barriers to entry for "high-risk suppliers"; on the other, it is reducing regulatory friction for suppliers from "like-minded countries." But feasibility does not hinge on Brussels' political will - it hinges on whether Europe can build replacement capacity within acceptable time and cost. For now, the answer is no, the expert said. European industry has bristled at EU plans to force businesses to diversify their supply chains away from China. According to a report by The South China Morning Post, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association said in a submission to the commission's request for evidence for DiversifyEU that "For rare earths, magnets, battery materials, displays and some semiconductors, there is little or no alternative supply base, and Europe lacks the ecosystem to provide one." "The objective should be realistic: Europe will not match Chinese costs or become fully independent of China, nor does it need to…" it noted. China-EU trade and economic consultations produced positive outcomes, which provide a stable environment for the bilateral trade and economic outlook. Yet the EU's "talk while fighting" approach exposes Brussels' short-sightedness, hypocrisy and self-contradiction in its China policy, Zhao Chen, senior research fellow at the Institute of European Studies under the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Wednesday. "Europe needs to face a reality: the deep interdependence of China-EU supply chains cannot be undone through regulatory maneuvering alone, and the cost of forcing such a breakup will fall first on European businesses and consumers," Zhao said. By talking cooperation on one hand while tripping the other side up on the other, the further this "dual-track" approach goes, the deeper the foundation of China-EU mutual trust will be eroded, and the narrower Europe's own room for development will become, Zhao warned.

item.title: Democrats win control of US Congress as voter discontent, Iran war weigh on outcome
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 23:34:00
Ballot processing workers prepare for the vote count that will begin after polls close at the Ballot Processing Center in City of Industry, California, US, on November 3, 2026. Photo: VCG Described by some US and European media as a "blue wave" or "blue tsunami," the 2026 US midterm election result showed Democrats were projected to win control of both chambers of Congress. As of early Wednesday morning, US time, Democrats were projected to win at least 245 House seats, with Republicans winning a minimum of 160 seats, according to the CNBC Election Desk. Democrats were also on track to hold at least 54 seats in the Senate, with Republicans likely to hold at least 42 seats. Chinese analysts observed that the results stem from voters' desire to "eliminate uncertainty," reflecting the "pendulum effect" in US politics rather than a broad endorsement of Democratic policy platforms. The post-election landscape may also point to deepening political infighting and societal polarization nationwide, they noted. Per NPR, the twin victories in the House and Senate "return the Democratic Party to full control of Congress for the first time since 2023 and deepen the level of expected friction between US President Donald Trump and congressional Democrats in a new era of divided government." Trump congratulated Democrats on their midterm election victories in a phone call with CBS News. "My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," he said. Reuters reported that House Speaker Mike Johnson said he was "disappointed" by the overwhelming gains made by Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections, but he vowed to battle on against what he called an "insurgent socialist movement." The Republicans' loss of full congressional control to the Democrats in the midterm elections may be attributed to the flawed domestic governance, marked by high inflation and swelling national debt that hurt ordinary Americans, especially young people, and undesirable foreign-policy results such as the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict and renewed tensions in the Middle East, Zhu Ying, a professor at the American research center of the Baize Institute at the Southwest University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times. Winning midterm elections is statistically rare for an incumbent president's party. Many voters cast ballots chiefly to ease Republican-driven national uncertainty. While a Democratic-led Congress may rein in Trump's proposals, it cannot drive fundamental US reform or fix deep-seated economic and living-standard woes, Zhu said. The outcome of these midterm elections largely reflects the "pendulum effect" in US politics, rather than a broad voter endorsement of Democratic policy agendas, Zhang Jiadong, a professor at the Center for American Studies, Fudan University, told the Global Times. Zhang noted that the political shifts brought by this election should not be overstated and to some extent, they merely represent normalcy in US politics. He noted that no single party can sustain popular approval for long, which is a phenomenon rooted in deeper-seated economic structural factors. According to an Associated Press report, Democratic control will profoundly reshape Trump's final two years in office and "hamstring his legislative agenda." Zhu noted that following the midterms, Congress will wield investigative powers amid mounting political infighting and social division. As societal polarization deepens in the US, rational centrist blocs have little room to gain traction and different groups may take sharply hardened stances on immigration, social regulation, religion and foreign policy issues. Trump admitted that the Iran war played a part in the midterm election results that saw Republicans taking a significant defeat, reported Fox News. The Iran war could reach an earlier conclusion, as the election outcome sends a clear message that US voters are against the war, some Chinese analysts noted. Zhang said a divided government could undermine the coherence and effectiveness of US foreign policy. While the president holds substantial authority over foreign and defense policy, advancing specific initiatives often requires congressional support. Democrats are likely to use their legislative and budgetary powers to pressure the Trump administration on issues including the Russia-Ukraine conflict. At the Chinese Foreign Ministry's regular press conference on Wednesday, a reporter asked how China viewed the recent US congressional elections and whether it saw any fresh possibilities in China-US relations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that the US midterm elections are a domestic affair. China stands ready to continue working with the US to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state, enhance communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity, said Mao. Zhu noted the Democrat-controlled Congress may strike louder rhetorical stances on issues such as human rights, technology and national-security issues. However, stable bilateral ties benefit all sides, as pressing global challenges demand joint solutions that take precedence over narrow domestic and geopolitical concerns.

item.title: From CIIE to whirlwind diplomatic engagements, China delivers development opportunities and stability amid global turmoil
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 23:18:00
CIIE Photo: VCG Amid simmering geopolitical tensions, rising trade protectionism and sweeping shifts in the global economic and security order, the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) is set to open in Shanghai on Thursday. China is also hosting a flurry of high-level visits of leaders from across Europe, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and Africa. These trade, development and security dialogues mark a significant milestone of China's major-country diplomacy. Analysts said that China leverages pragmatic bilateral diplomatic consultations and multilateral platforms to coordinate trade cooperation and regional security agendas. It delivers development dividends and stabilizing momentum, signaling its commitment to multilateralism, open cooperation and win‑win outcomes with all countries. Deliver new opportunities The ninth CIIE will be held from November 5 to 10 in Shanghai, bringing together exhibitors from around the world. Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE has become an important gateway for foreign businesses seeking access to China's vast consumer and industrial markets. According to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), this year's expo is expected to attract 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 148 countries and regions, including more than 2,000 first-time exhibitors. Overall, 162 countries, regions and international organizations will participate. Companies from the US, Germany, UK and France will occupy the largest exhibition areas. Meanwhile, the expo has expanded support for the world's least-developed countries, increasing the free exhibition space allocated to them by 17 percent from last year, when more than 160 companies from 37 such countries participated. "The CIIE has become an inspiring platform for us to exchange, listen, learn, and work with our partners… What I especially appreciate about the CIIE is that it brings together government, industry, researchers, entrepreneurs, and companies from around the world," Bill Anderson, Chairman of the Board of Management of Bayer AG, told the Global Times on Wednesday. "Bayer is deeply committed to continue fostering innovation and collaboration in China," he added. According to Huo Jianguo, former head of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under MOFCOM, the CIIE fully demonstrates China's resolve to keep its market open and pursue mutually beneficial international cooperation. As unilateralism and protectionism repeatedly batter the international economic and trade order, the CIIE has become an irreplaceable global public good within the world trade system. He noted that the expo reflects China's stance in pursuing trade balance, rebutting some Western smears regarding China's trade surplus. "China does not aim for sustained trade surpluses or focus solely on expanding exports. Rather, it taps into its huge domestic market to steadily deliver development opportunities worldwide," Huo remarked. "By taking the initiative to boost imports and cooperating with trade partners to reinvigorate global trade, China puts into practice its vision of common development." For 17 consecutive years, China has remained the world's second-largest importer. Also in the first three quarters of 2026, the country's imports rose 22.3 percent year-on-year, significantly outpacing export growth, the Xinhua News Agency reported. According to the People's Daily, China has contributed around 30 percent to global economic growth for years. It has signed Belt and Road cooperation documents with more than 150 countries and over 30 international organizations. Following the CIIE, China will host another major multilateral economic and trade event in November. Shenzhen, in South China's Guangdong Province, will host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19. The theme of this year's summit is "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," while China has identified openness, innovation and cooperation as the three priority areas for this year's APEC cooperation. While co-chairing the 37th APEC Ministerial Meeting via video conference with Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao on Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi called on members to uphold mutual respect, deepen solidarity, foster an open environment and sustain the momentum of integration. Wang Wentao said that China will always stay committed to promoting high-level opening up. He added that the APEC parties should continue to contribute practical and effective "Asia-Pacific solutions" to the development of the Asia-Pacific region and the world at large. Saravoot Yoovidhya, CEO of Thailand's TCP Group, told the Global Times on Wednesday that the APEC economies constitute a key source of exhibitors at the CIIE. By continuously unlocking opportunities of China's vast market, the expo has become a vital gateway for Asia-Pacific exhibitors to expand into the Chinese market and deepen regional cooperation. As a champion of regional cooperation and a major engine of the global economy, China brings much-needed certainty to Asia-Pacific cooperation and prosperity. An open, inclusive and mutually beneficial environment for regional cooperation delivers stable institutional expectations for multinational enterprises like TCP Group, he added. Anchor of stability Foreign dignitaries including Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema and Austrian Federal Chancellor Christian Stocker are among the foreign leaders attending the CIIE in Shanghai. They join the recent wave of foreign dignitaries from Europe, the Middle East and Southeast Asia to visit China. Analysts pointed out that peace and development are the common aspirations of all countries. This latest surge of China's home-based multilateral and bilateral diplomacy integrates trade, diplomatic and security agendas, offering a rare source of stability for the global community. "China pursues proactive, unilateral and institutional opening-up. The development it advocates goes beyond sustainable development and emphasizes shared development," Wang Yiwei, a professor at the School of International Studies at the Renmin University of China, told the Global Times on Wednesday. Amid today's shifting global landscape, many countries are seeking deeper cooperation with China, attracted by its commitment to openness and inclusiveness, the expert noted. "This stands in sharp contrast to the closed, exclusive and internationally irresponsible approach of the US, as well as the trend of rising protectionism in Europe amid populist pressures." Meanwhile, in carrying out international cooperation, China consistently adheres to the principles of non-interference in internal affairs, non-alignment and not coercing other countries into taking sides, delivering rare security and predictable expectations amid a turbulent global landscape, he added.

item.title: 2026 Kuliang Forum opens in Fuzhou, spotlighting lasting bonds between Chinese and American people
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 22:38:00
The 2026 Kuliang Forum kicks off in Fuzhou, East China's Fujian Province, on November 4, 2026. Source: Courtesy of People's Daily Digital Communication Co., Ltd. The 2026 Kuliang Forum, organized by People's Daily Digital Communication Co., Ltd., opened in Fuzhou, East China's Fujian Province, on Wednesday, bringing together guests from China and the US to explore ways to strengthen people-to-people ties and advance practical cooperation. For the first time, the forum was held in the city where the century-old Kuliang story began. Under the theme of "Moving Towards Each Other," participants at this year's forum shared their perspectives on the history and future of China-US friendship, how language and cultural exchanges can bring people closer, and the importance of providing young people with more opportunities to meet, learn from and work with one another. At the opening ceremony on Wednesday morning, Yu Shaoliang, president of People's Daily, said that as a flagship platform for people-to-people and cultural exchanges between China and the US, this year's forum would bring together forces for closer engagement and open new paths for cooperation, friendship and the future. He expressed hope that people from all sectors in both countries would be guided by the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, share more stories of friendship, voice greater support for cooperation, and deepen mutual understanding and mutual trust. He also called on media organizations, think tanks, universities, businesses and local communities in both countries to use the forum as a bridge for deeper exchanges and cooperation in education, science and technology, trade and culture, encouraging more frequent visits and interactions between the two peoples and helping them build closer ties. Through sincere dialogue and exchanges, he said, the two sides should work to deliver more practical results that benefit the people of both countries and contribute to global development, achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, and further strengthen the momentum for China-US friendship. Zhao Long, secretary of the Fujian Provincial Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC), and Qin Haixiang, secretary of the Fuzhou Municipal Committee of the CPC, also attended the forum and delivered remarks. US participants highlighted how language learning, shared experiences and everyday interactions help build personal connections. "People-to-people exchanges should not be like visiting an aquarium," said Eric Chipman, executive director of the Helen Foster Snow Foundation and Gung Ho Programs, speaking in Chinese at the forum. He argued that genuine connections could only be built when people went beyond observing one another and found opportunities to take part in each other's lives and work toward shared goals. In an interview with the Global Times, Chipman said a major challenge was Americans' limited exposure to China. Drawing on his nearly two decades of experience organizing China-US exchange programs, he said firsthand experiences could profoundly change young people's perspectives. "When they come here, they can't view the world the same way ever again," he said, adding that some former student participants had gone on to study or work in China or encourage others to visit. Chipman described Kuliang's history as a reminder of the long-standing connections between the two countries. He also expressed interest in bringing American students to Kuliang in the future, saying, "That would be incredible." Other US participants also shared their thoughts on how to foster understanding between the two peoples, drawing on their own experiences and areas of interest. Trenton Marsolek, a 27-year-old Tsinghua University alumnus, visited Kuliang for the first time during the trip. He told the Global Times that the Kuliang story and the friendship it represents carry significant meaning for China-US relations. He said friendships between Chinese and American people had endured through changing historical circumstances. To promote greater mutual understanding, Marsolek said more young Americans should visit China and experience the country firsthand. He said young people did not need to begin conversations with complicated political or philosophical topics. "At the end of the day, we're all human," he said, adding that conversations about ordinary topics help people see one another as individuals and build mutual understanding. For Vivian, a Chinese-American student at Peking University's School of Chinese as a Second Language, the forum was particularly meaningful given her work in teaching Chinese to international students. She told the Global Times that language learning cannot be separated from culture, real-life settings and stories. The forum offers American students and other visitors an opportunity not only to learn about Kuliang and its history, but also to experience Chinese culture firsthand. Drawing on her experience in Chinese language education, Vivian stressed that people need to interact with one another in order to develop genuine understanding. Such exchanges, she said, can help American students and business visitors gain a deeper appreciation of Chinese culture. This year's forum also featured roundtable discussions and youth exchange activities. Participants discussed the importance of constructive relations between major countries, the lessons of history for China-US relations and ways to deepen friendship between the two peoples. During the event, a new book, Bond with Kuliang: Stories of China-US Friendship and Cooperation , was launched, while an accompanying photo exhibition was held featuring images documenting exchanges and friendship between people in China and the US. Since its launch in 2024, the Kuliang Forum has held two editions in Beijing and New York, bringing together more than 300 participants from various sectors in China and the US. The forum has become a platform for dialogue and exchange between people from both countries.

item.title: GT Voice: Why resisting US pressure matters for South Korean chipmakers
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 22:26:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG Washington's efforts to attract South Korean chip investment risk being undermined by its own restrictions. Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that US officials have held up approval for American chipmaking equipment needed by SK hynix to expand its production in China, complicating the South Korean chipmaker's plans for new memory-chip plants in the state of New York. According to Reuters, SK hynix is seeking US export licenses to equip its plant in Dalian, Northeast China's Liaoning Province, arguing that increased production there would help fund its planned US expansion. Negotiations are ongoing, with the outcome uncertain. But the episode already exposes tension in US-South Korea chip "cooperation." Washington wants to attract more South Korean investment and manufacturing capacity to the US, while its export controls constrain South Korean chipmakers' ability to expand its production in China. This reveals a divergence of interests: Washington is seeking to strengthen its own semiconductor industry, even at the potential expense of South Korean companies' commercial interests. For a fuller picture of the pressure facing South Korean chipmakers, a September report by The Korea Herald is worth revisiting. It said that Washington had revived its push for targeted semiconductor tariffs, raising pressure on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to expand US production or face duties on chips made overseas. If South Korean chipmakers expand their US operations under such pressure, a growing share of investment, advanced manufacturing capacity and high-value jobs could accrue to the US rather than South Korea. This raises a question about whether such "cooperation" truly serves both sides' interests. Washington stands to gain new investment and jobs, while South Korean companies face constraints on their global operations and risk seeing more of their industrial capabilities move overseas. The arrangement appears to put US industrial interests first, leaving South Korea to bear much of the commercial and strategic cost. On its US investment plans, South Korean media outlet AJP reported on Wednesday that SK hynix had yet to finalize any specific plans for new semiconductor manufacturing facilities in the US. SK hynix also said that it was continuing to bring US-made semiconductor manufacturing equipment into its Dalian plant under an existing export license, while negotiations over next year's authorization remain underway, AJP reported. Why are these Chinese factories so important to South Korean chipmakers? The Korea JoongAng Daily reported in August that SK hynix's plant in Wuxi, East China's Jiangsu Province, accounts for 40 percent of its total dynamic random-access memory output, while its Dalian plant accounts for 30 percent of its total NAND output. At a time of strong global demand and tight memory-chip supply, China's production capacity is a valuable asset for South Korean chipmakers. Retaining access to this capacity is plainly in the commercial interests of these companies. China's value also lies in its mature industrial ecosystem. Its extensive supplier networks and manufacturing capabilities have long supported South Korean chipmakers' global operations. This has been a mutually beneficial arrangement, with South Korean companies drawing on China's industrial base while contributing investment to the wider supply chain. Yet Washington is putting South Korean chipmakers in a difficult position. While seeking to attract their investment to the US, it is also trying to limit their ability to expand production in China. In doing so, Washington is putting its geopolitical objectives ahead of South Korean companies' commercial interests. South Korean chipmakers should not accommodate US demands at the expense of their global operations. They have every reason to preserve the flexibility to make investment and production decisions based on commercial considerations. China's semiconductor industry is advancing rapidly, creating new competitive pressures for South Korean chipmakers. But competition does not preclude cooperation where interests remain aligned. The question is whether South Korean chipmakers can withstand US pressure without sacrificing the global reach and commercial flexibility on which their competitiveness depends. That balance will have consequences well beyond their operations in China.

item.title: 9-year CIIE: An open China responds to surge of protectionism with tangible dividends
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 20:41:00
A ceremony marking the arrival of the first batch of exhibits for the upcoming 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) is held at the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai), the main venue for the CIIE, in east China's Shanghai on October 26, 2026. Photo: Xinhua On November 5, the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) will kick off in Shanghai. The fact that the event has been held as scheduled for nine consecutive years is, in itself, a powerful declaration of openness. This year's expo brings together 162 countries, regions, and international organizations, with 4,142 overseas companies participating. For the first time, the number of Fortune 500 companies and industry leaders among the exhibitors has exceeded 300, and nearly 200 companies and institutions have participated in all nine editions of the expo. One of the most intriguing highlights of this year's CIIE comes from the US delegation. For the eighth consecutive year, US companies have occupied the largest exhibition space among all participating countries, with their exhibition area increasing by another 1,500 square meters compared to the previous edition. Even as Washington's policy toolkit is filled with tariff barriers and "small yards, high fences" approach, US companies continue to showcase cutting-edge innovations on this platform, aiming to foster a mutually beneficial relationship with the Chinese market. "The power of the market is robust," said Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce. "US companies are not just chasing short-term gains by participating in the expo; they are also exploring opportunities for deeper cooperation. Amid global market volatility and supply chain pressures, China boasts both growth potential and supply chain resilience. That explains the core reason behind this contrast - "policymakers build walls, yet businesses show up." World premieres and first-time exhibitions are the most distinctive hallmarks of the CIIE. During the first eight sessions of the CIIE, more than 3,400 new products, technologies, and services made their global or regional debuts. This year, there are over 480 representative exhibits making their global, Asian, or China debuts - a record high - which reflects this mutual engagement in innovation. Zhou Mi told the Global Times that innovation is key for companies to generate profits and capture market share. The decision to launch a large number of new products in China stems from the potential of the Chinese market and its advantages in industrial support systems. Tu Xinquan, Dean of the China Institute for WTO Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, believes that as one of the world's largest consumer markets, China ranks among the global leaders in domestic consumer acceptance of new technologies and products. Making China the launchpad, testing ground, and promotion hub for their innovations is a highly strategic choice for innovative enterprises. The appeal of the CIIE also stems from tangible orders and growth dividends. The cumulative intended transaction value from the first eight editions exceeded $580 billion, with the eighth edition alone recording $83.49 billion in intended transactions - a 4.4 percent year-over-year increase. Take Takeda Pharmaceutical as an example. From a mid-sized company at its first exhibition, it has grown into one of the top 10 multinational pharmaceutical companies in China, with cumulative investment in the country exceeding 3 billion yuan. Turning exhibits into products and exhibitors into investors represents the tangible, concrete, and graspable opportunities in China for the global business community. Tu believes that China is committed to independent, high-level opening-up, and the CIIE serves as a key window through which China proactively embraces the world. "At a time when anti-globalization sentiments are on the rise and global trade and the economy are fraught with uncertainty, China has continued to host the expo year after year, injecting stability into turbulent global trade and serving as a stabilizer for the world economy," Tu said. He added that the CIIE also builds a bridge connecting high-quality international supply with domestic consumption upgrades, driving the optimization of domestic supply and unleashing the potential of domestic consumption. "It is hoped that China's practice of opening up will inspire more countries to safeguard the multilateral free trade system." The CIIE's cooperative philosophy is based on equality and mutual benefit, without distinction by nationality or alignment with any bloc: Developed countries showcase cutting-edge technologies, emerging markets demonstrate their vibrant dynamism, and least-developed economies receive support here. This year's event continues to support least developed countries, with the amount of free exhibition space allocated to them increasing by 17 percent year-on-year; distinctive agricultural products from African nations such as Tanzania and Benin have found stable sales channels here. Rwanda is a prime example. The country went from bringing samples in a suitcase to now shipping a steady stream of local agricultural products to China by container. Developed economies, emerging markets, and least developed countries are all participating on an equal footing, standing in stark contrast to exclusive, "closed-circle" economic and trade arrangements. Zhou said the CIIE provides a platform for countries to exchange ideas and learn from one another, where different stakeholders can engage in dialogue and inspire each other. This diverse and inclusive framework is a concrete demonstration of China's commitment to treating all trading partners equally, upholding the principle of most-favored-nation treatment. Over the past five years, China's contribution to global economic growth has remained stable at around 30 percent, exceeding the combined contribution of the G7 nations. Today's "China Opportunities 2.0" places greater emphasis on innovation and collaboration, institutional openness, and full-chain co-construction. The continuously expanding scale of the US delegation at the expo confirms a simple truth: Businesses vote with their feet, and market forces are difficult to completely block with geopolitical barriers. The value of the CIIE's 9-year commitment lies in its steadfastness. While tariffs can artificially inflate transaction costs, they cannot stem the drive of global capital, innovation, and goods to find markets. The message the CIIE continues to send is clear and resolute: The doors to the Chinese market will remain open to all partners willing to cooperate on an equal footing.

item.title: Scholars from around the world trace Silk Road history in Xinjiang
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 12:43:00
A scholar from Pakistan shares research findings at the symposium titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, in Urumqi, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yuanhao) Once a thriving crossroads on the Silk Road in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the ancient kingdom of Kucha has left traces of its rich history in museums and collections around the world. Buddhist murals, sculptures and manuscripts from the Kucha kingdom, also known as the ancient Qiuci State ("Qiuci" being its Chinese pinyin form), are now held in Berlin, St. Petersburg, Tokyo and elsewhere. Reconstructing its past is therefore requiring researchers to work across borders and pool their expertise. Understanding Kucha's past has become an international scholarly effort. The shared pursuit brought more than 180 scholars from 15 countries and regions to Urumqi, capital of Xinjiang, for a two-day symposium, titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, which concluded on Sunday. Scholars from China, Britain, Germany, Italy, Japan, Pakistan and elsewhere exchanged research findings on ancient texts, religion, archaeology and cultural heritage conservation. Located between the Tianshan Mountains and the Taklimakan Desert, the ancient Kucha region encompassed parts of today's Kuqa, Baicheng, Xayar and Xinhe in Xinjiang. For centuries, it was a meeting point of civilizations. Chinese silk and paper traveled westward along trade routes, while Buddhism from India, Persian artistic influences and Sogdian merchants made their way east. At the symposium, Rong Xinjiang, a professor at Peking University and president of the Chinese Dunhuang-Turpan Society, presented new research on a tomb epitaph unearthed in Kuqa in 2025. For overseas researchers, keeping up with archaeological discoveries in Xinjiang is an important reason to maintain close ties with Chinese scholars. "Continued contact with colleagues around the world, especially in China, is essential," said Caren Dreyer, a researcher at the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin. "It enables us to keep abreast of new findings and to participate actively in the international scholarly community." For Erica Hunter, a scholar from the University of Cambridge who specializes in relics and Syriac manuscripts excavated from Turpan, the value of such gatherings lies in bringing together evidence that would otherwise remain separated by geography. Russian scholars can share materials from St. Petersburg, while German researchers can discuss those in Berlin, Hunter said. Equally important are the different interpretations scholars bring to their research. Hunter has visited Xinjiang several times over the past four years to share her research on Syriac manuscripts discovered in the region. She said such exchanges help scholars overcome barriers and learn from one another. "It's a two-way process, and that's very important." On his first visit to Xinjiang, Pakistani scholar Fawad Khan followed the presentations with keen interest. He said the symposium offered a valuable learning opportunity for scholars. The exchanges also reflected a growing emphasis on international collaboration in Silk Road studies, as Chinese institutions expand academic cooperation in fields ranging from Turpan and Qiuci studies, to research on the ancient city of Beiting. For Italian scholar Erica Forte, the symposium was also a reunion. Speaking Chinese with colleagues, she caught up with old friends and professors who had supported her during her studies. For her, the conversations reflected what had long given the Silk Road its significance, namely connections between people and cultures, as scholars came together to exchange findings, compare perspectives and deepen their understanding of a kingdom that once stood at the crossroads of civilizations. Erica Hunter, a scholar from the University of Cambridge, attends the symposium titled Towards Anxi from Afar: Academic Symposium on Qiuci Studies, in Urumqi, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Yuanhao)

item.title: China stocks surge as policy support boosts sentiment; AI tech shares lead rally
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 11:00:00
The People's Bank of China Photo: VCG Chinese equities staged a powerful rebound on Wednesday, buoyed by supportive policies aimed at stabilizing the capital markets and boosting investor confidence, with artificial intelligence (AI) and technology shares leading the surge. The STAR Composite Index, which reflects the performance of stocks on China's sci-tech innovation board, closed 9.9 percent higher at 1,525.31 points. More than 150 stocks on the sci-tech innovation board hit their daily price limit or gained more than 10 percent, reflecting broad-based buying across the technology sector, according to the Securities Times. Among the standout performers, CXMT jumped 13.63 percent, with turnover exceeding 20 billion yuan ($2.99 billion). The rally was accompanied by a sharp increase in trading activity, with total A-share turnover reached 2.0519 trillion yuan, up 336.8 billion yuan from the previous trading session. More than 4,600 stocks advanced on the day. Market observers said that the sharp rally was supported by coordinated policy efforts by multiple government departments to stabilize market expectations and boost investor confidence. Previously, the People's Bank of China (PBC), the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the China Securities Regulatory Commission held two separate meetings aimed at stabilizing the capital market. In addition, other coordinated measures have been introduced to bolster market liquidity and confidence. The PBC, China's central bank, said on Wednesday that it has stepped up the implementation of stock repurchase and share buy-back relending policies, cutting the relending facility rate by 25 basis points to 1 percent effective immediately, in an attempt to maintain stable operation of the country's capital market. The facility is available to 21 national-level commercial banks and five systemically important city-level banks. It covers 100 percent of eligible loans, has a term of one year and can be extended according to the banks' needs, according to a PBC announcement on Wednesday. Banks are allowed to add a reasonable margin on top of the relending rate and independently determine the maturities and pricing of loans for stock repurchases and shareholding increases. They are encouraged to accelerate loan disbursements and enhance listed companies' and major shareholders' capacity for market value management, the PBC said. According to Li Chang'an, a professor at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies at the University of International Business and Economics, lowering the interest rate on stock repurchases and the relending facility carries multiple positive implications for the market. Li told the Global Times on Wednesday that the move would reduce financing costs for listed companies, making it easier for them to repurchase shares and increase holdings at a time when capital markets remain relatively weak, helping to support stability in the stock and securities markets. The central bank also pledged to provide sufficient relending quota, a move that experts said would release more liquidity and draw additional funds into equities, further bolstering market confidence. Following several meetings on the program on Monday, banks submitted quota applications totaling more than 200 billion yuan, and the PBC said that it will continue to fully meet banks' relending needs and support them in actively addressing the financing demand of listed companies and major shareholders, according to the statement. As long-term capital gradually enters the market, the medium- to long-term outlook remains positive. Li added that banks and brokerages have responded positively, with applications for repurchase and shareholding increase relending quotas continuing to rise, signaling strong interest in supporting market stability. However, he emphasized that long-term market stability depends on deeper institutional reforms, including stricter IPO screening, improved delisting mechanisms and better dividend policies, so that higher-quality listed companies can deliver sustainable returns and provide a stronger foundation for the market. Wednesday's rate cut followed an announcement by the PBC earlier this week to shift the relending program from a temporary arrangement to a permanent institutional arrangement, and lower the relending rate from 1.25 percent to 1 percent. The program is one of two policy tools supporting the capital market, alongside the Securities, Funds and Insurance Companies Swap Facility. Industry analysts said that the latest PBC measures are fresh moves to support the stable and healthy development of the capital market. They are expected to channel more funds into the stock market by helping financial institutions expand their investment capacity, while broader participation by institutional investors could help strengthen market confidence. On Wednesday, Chinese chipmaker CXMT announced a fresh plan to raise the amount of its share repurchase. Under the proposed adjustment, the buyback amount would increase from the original range of 1 billion yuan to 2 billion yuan, to a new range of 2.5 billion yuan to 5 billion yuan, with both the floor and ceiling 2.5 times the original plan and the upper limit increased by 3 billion yuan. The company said that the proposal reflects its confidence in its future sustainable development and its strong recognition of the company's value. The move is intended to protect investors' interests, strengthen market confidence, and support the company's stable and healthy growth. "It is both necessary and beneficial to use policy tools such as stock repurchase and related refinancing to inject liquidity into the market," Dong Shaopeng, a senior research fellow at the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University of China, told the Global Times on Wednesday. The expert also rejected foreign media claims that China's stock market volatility is mainly driven by external shocks, structural economic pressures and sell-offs in the technology and AI sectors. He said that the volatility is largely a result of domestic market dynamics. As most Chinese listed companies remain heavily reliant on the domestic market, corporate earnings and operating efficiency are key factors underpinning the equity market. The market is expected to gradually shift from sentiment-driven trading to performance driven by fundamentals. As the foundation of China's economic recovery continues to strengthen, corporate earnings are expected to improve steadily, providing fundamental support for the equity market, according to Chinese analysts. Wednesday's rally reflected both a technical rebound from oversold conditions and a policy-driven improvement in expectations, Yang Delong, chief economist at Shenzhen-based First Seafront Fund, told the Global Times. Yang said that the coordinated measures have significantly eased downward pressure and could help Chinese equities gradually recover.
